title: Generic cohomology and localization boundary in the tame trait model
statement:
Let $\ell$ be a prime, $n\geq1$, $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, and $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$ for a strictly henselian discrete valuation ring on which $\ell$ is invertible [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. Write $s$ and $\eta$ for its closed and generic points, $j:\eta\hookrightarrow T$, and choose a geometric generic point $\bar\eta$ [def-weil-geometric-point]. Let $H=\operatorname{Gal}(\kappa(\bar\eta)/\kappa(\eta))$, its tame quotient $G$ with pro-$p$ kernel $S$, $A=\Lambda[[G]]$, its augmentation ideal $I$, and the exact functor $F$ be as in [lem-per-prime-power-trait-residue-model]; supported sections are [def-pur-etale-derived-supported-sections]. For a bounded below complex $K$ of sheaves of $\Lambda$-modules on $T_{\mathrm{et}}$, let $C(K)$ be the total complex of the double complex whose $q$-th row is $K^q_{\bar\eta}{}^S\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,K^q_{\bar\eta}{}^S)$, $m\mapsto(a\mapsto am)$, placed in degrees $0,1$. Fix $F(K)\simeq R\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,K)$ by choosing a bounded below injective replacement $K\to J$ and inverting the quasi-isomorphism induced by the evident map $\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,J)\to F(J)$, $h\mapsto(h,0,0)$ (the “morphisme évident” of ILO XVII 1.2.2.1), using also $F(K)\simeq F(J)$. Then:

(a) The functor $C$ is exact termwise, and there is an isomorphism $C(K)\simeq R\Gamma(\eta,K|_\eta)$ in $D^+(\Lambda)$ [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories], natural in $K$. For a single sheaf $M$ it is the identity $M_{\bar\eta}^H=\ker(M_{\bar\eta}^S\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,M_{\bar\eta}^S))$ in degree zero, and in degree one it sends the class of the $A$-linear map $f_c$ to the inflation to $H$ of the class of the continuous crossed homomorphism $c:G\to M_{\bar\eta}^S$ with $f_c(g-1)=c(g)$, the comparison of [lem-per-augmentation-cocycle-comparison] (continuous cohomology as in [def-exc-continuous-cohomology]).

(b) Global sections on $T$ are the closed geometric stalk, $\Gamma(T,M)=M_s$, so $R\Gamma(T,K)\simeq K_s$. Inclusion of the two generic columns and projection to the closed-stalk column give a degreewise split exact sequence of complexes $0\to C(K)[-1]\to F(K)\to K_s\to0$, natural in $K$. Under (a), the identification of $F(K)$ above and $R\Gamma(T,K)\simeq K_s$, its distinguished triangle is isomorphic to the triangle obtained by applying derived global sections to the localization triangle of [lem-exc-closed-support-triangle] for $s\hookrightarrow T\hookleftarrow\eta$, with identity on all three vertices. The two connecting maps $R\Gamma(\eta,K|_\eta)\to R\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,K)[1]$ agree up to a sign $\epsilon_0\in\{1,-1\}$ that depends only on the fixed cone and total-complex sign conventions, not on $T$, $K$ or a generator of $G$. In particular the localization boundary sends the class of a degree-$(m+1)$ cocycle $(0,x)$ of $C(K)$, with $x\in\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,K^m_{\bar\eta}{}^S)$, to the class of $\epsilon_0x$ in the degree-two column of $F(K)$.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1-1.2.2: Proposition 1.2.1.2 and the proof of Proposition 1.2.2.1 (the kernel of M_eta^S -> Hom(I_G, M_eta^S) is Gamma(eta, M); F(M) is the fibre of M_s over the generic two-term complex), printed pp. 259-260; used in the omitted verification of Lemma 3.6.2, p. 279

proof.text: Put $W(M)=M_s$, $N(M)=M_{\bar\eta}^S$, $P(M)=\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,N(M))$, and $t(v)(a)=av$. These are exactly the three degree functors of the exact functor $F$ in [lem-per-prime-power-trait-residue-model], so each is exact: evaluating a short exact sequence of complexes in a fixed degree is exact. In particular $C(M)=[N(M)\xrightarrow{t}P(M)]$ is exact termwise. The specialization $a:W(M)\to N(M)$ has image in $M_{\bar\eta}^H$, by [lem-per-trait-sheaf-gluing], hence $ta=0$. By freeness $I=A(1-\sigma)$ in the residue-model statement, $t(v)=0$ iff $(1-\sigma)v=0$. An element of a discrete continuous module fixed by $\sigma$ is fixed by $G$: its closed stabilizer contains the dense powers of $\sigma$. Thus $\ker t=N(M)^G=M_{\bar\eta}^H=\Gamma(\eta,M|_\eta)$, the last equality being precisely the generic-sections clause of the gluing statement.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text:
Fix the total differential $d_h+(-1)^i d_K$ in horizontal degree $i$, and shifts $d_{L[1]}=-d_L$ as in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. In degree $r$ write $C(K)^r=N(K^r)\oplus P(K^{r-1})$ and $F(K)^r=W(K^r)\oplus N(K^{r-1})\oplus P(K^{r-2})$. Their differentials are
$$D_C(v,x)=(dv,tv-dx),\qquad D_F(w,v,x)=(dw,aw-dv,tv+dx).$$
Projection $q(w,v,x)=w$ is a chain map, with kernel identified with $C(K)[-1]$ by $\iota(v,x)=(0,v,-x)$. Indeed $D_F\iota(v,x)=(0,-dv,tv-dx)=\iota(-D_C(v,x))$. The maps $w\mapsto(w,0,0)$ split $q$ in each degree. This gives the claimed natural degreewise split short exact sequence; the word inclusion includes the displayed shift sign. If $r_K:W(K)\to C(K)$ sends $w$ to $(aw,0)$, then $(w,v,x)\mapsto((-v,x),w)$ is a chain isomorphism $F(K)\to\operatorname{Cone}(r_K)[-1]$, by the cone differential in the cited definition.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text: The category of $\Lambda$-module sheaves on $T_{\mathrm{et}}$ is Grothendieck abelian by [lem-weil-pbc-module-sheaves-grothendieck-abelian] and has enough injectives by [lem-sp-grothendieck-enough-injectives]. Choose $K\to J$ bounded below and injective termwise by [lem-sc-bounded-below-injective-resolution-existence]. In the triples of [lem-per-trait-sheaf-gluing], restriction to $\eta$ is $(W,V,a)\mapsto V$ and has exact left adjoint $V\mapsto(0,V,0)$: maps out of this triple are exactly equivariant maps out of $V$, and exactness is componentwise. Therefore restriction takes injective sheaves to injective sheaves on $\eta$ by [lem-exc-rg-right-adjoint-preserves-injectives]. Consequently $\Gamma(\eta,J|_\eta)$ computes $R\Gamma(\eta,K|_\eta)$ by [lem-weil-pbc-right-derived-plus-injective]. All these are ordinary bounded below module derived categories; no constructibility or finite generation is required.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text: For an injective sheaf $E$, [lem-per-prime-power-trait-residue-model] and [def-pur-etale-derived-supported-sections] give $H^rF(E)=0$ for $r>0$: the complex consisting of $E$ in degree zero is itself an injective resolution for supported sections. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-complex-ses-homology-long-exact] to Step 2 with $K=E[0]$. Since $W(E)[0]$ has no positive cohomology, it gives $H^1C(E)=H^2F(E)=0$. The two-term complex $C(E)$ has no cohomology above degree one, and Step 1 identifies its degree-zero kernel. Thus the canonical augmentation $\Gamma(\eta,E|_\eta)[0]\to C(E)$ is a quasi-isomorphism, with degree-zero component the inclusion of invariants. This obtains generic injective acyclicity from the stated supported-cohomology theorem, without borrowing any argument hidden in that theorem's proof.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text: Exactness of $N$ and $P$ means that $N(K)\to N(J)$ and $P(K)\to P(J)$ are quasi-isomorphisms: an exact additive functor preserves kernels, images and their cohomology quotients. Apply [lem-sc-integer-finite-column-total-comparison] with horizontal bounds $0,1$ to obtain $C(K)\xrightarrow{\sim}C(J)$. Each diagonal has just two summands, so the totals exist even when the lower bound of $K$ is negative. Step 4 supplies the row quasi-isomorphisms needed in [lem-sc-finite-strip-row-augmentation], with strip width $2$ and $A^q=\Gamma(\eta,J^q|_\eta)$. Its augmentation is a chain map because inclusion of invariants is natural and $t$ kills invariants. Hence $\Gamma(\eta,J|_\eta)\xrightarrow{\sim}C(J)$. Together with Step 3 this gives the natural comparison $C(K)\simeq R\Gamma(\eta,K|_\eta)$. Naturality is that of these augmentations and of the right-derived comparison [lem-weil-pbc-right-derived-plus-injective]; replacing an injective resolution gives the same isomorphism after localization. Its $H^0$ is the identity of Step 1.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text: We check the degree-one normalization, rather than choosing an arbitrary isomorphism of cohomology groups. For a sheaf $M$ with generic module $V$ and $N=V^S$, send $v\in N$ to $v\in V$ in continuous cochain degree zero and send $f\in\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,N)$ to $h\mapsto f(\bar h-1)$ in degree one, where $\bar h$ is the tame image of $h\in H$; in higher degrees the source is zero. The map $I\to N$ is continuous by the completed action in [def-per-completed-augmentation-algebra] and the following finite calculation. Put $x=f(1-\sigma)$, choose $d$ prime to the residue characteristic exponent with $\sigma^d x=x$, and put $e=\ell^n d$. In $B_e=\Lambda[G/\overline{\langle\sigma^e\rangle}]$, coefficient comparison gives $\ker(1-z)=\Lambda(1+z+\cdots+z^{e-1})$. If $y=(1-\sigma)b\in I$ has zero $B_e$-coordinate, then $b_e$ is a multiple of this norm and $f(y)=bx=0$, since the norm acts by $\ell^n\sum_{i<d}\sigma^ix=0$. Thus $f$ kills the open kernel of $I\to B_e$ and is continuous. The cocycle identity follows from $gh-1=(g-1)+g(h-1)$, and $f_{t(v)}(h)=hv-v$, so these maps commute with differentials and are natural coefficient maps. By [lem-per-augmentation-cocycle-comparison] the degree-one map sends exactly $f_c$ to the inflation of $c$, with $f_c(1-\sigma)=-c(\sigma)$.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text: The comparisons of Steps 5 and 6 must respect coefficient boundaries. Given $0\to M'\to M\to M''\to0$, choose nonnegative injective resolutions $J',J''$ and a prescribed horseshoe $0\to J'\to J\to J''\to0$ by [lem-sp-horseshoe-prescribed-resolutions]. It is split in every degree. Restriction to $\eta$ preserves injectives by Step 3, so $B_X=\Gamma(\eta,J_X|_\eta)$ form a termwise exact sequence computing generic derived sections. By [lem-weil-pbc-horseshoe-delta-functor] its connecting maps are independent of this choice and give the derived-invariants delta-functor of [def-exc-continuous-cohomology] under [lem-per-trait-sheaf-gluing]. Both arrows $C(M_X)\to C(J_X)\leftarrow B_X$ in Step 5 give commuting maps of termwise exact sequences: exactness of $C$ handles the first sequence; splitness of the horseshoe handles the latter two. Naturality of the connecting construction in [lem-weil-pbc-complex-ses-triangle] (followed by cohomology) makes this zigzag a morphism of delta-functors. Step 6 is a natural cochain map on coefficient short exact sequences, so it also respects the connecting maps of [lem-exc-continuous-cochains-delta-functor]. The delta-functor $H^*C$ is effaceable: injective embeddings from Step 3 kill its positive groups by Step 4. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-effaceable-delta-functor-universal] makes the two comparisons equal, since both are the identity on $V^H$. This proves precisely the degree-one inflation normalization in (a).

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text:
By [lem-per-trait-sheaf-gluing], $\Gamma(T,M)=W(M)$ naturally and $W$ is exact (kernels and cokernels are componentwise). Thus $W(K)\to W(J)$ is a quasi-isomorphism, and the computation on injectives in [lem-weil-pbc-right-derived-plus-injective] gives $R\Gamma(T,K)=K_s$. For an injective triple $E=(W,V,a)$ the map $a:W\to V^H$ is onto: given $v\in V^H$, the map $(0,\Lambda,0)\to E$ sending $1$ to $v$ extends along the monomorphism $(0,\Lambda,0)\to(\Lambda,\Lambda,\mathrm{id})$. The closed component of the extension lifts $v$. Its kernel is $\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,E)$ by [def-pur-etale-derived-supported-sections]. Applying this in every degree of $J$ gives a natural short exact sequence
$$0\to\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,J)\to W(J)\to\Gamma(\eta,J|_\eta)\to0.$$
The degree-zero restriction is exactly $a$, not a different comparison map.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text: We first model the localization vertices and first two arrows. In triples, $i_*U=(U,0,0)$ and $j_*V=(V^H,V,\mathrm{incl})$: the adjunctions follow from $\operatorname{Hom}(i_*U,M)=\operatorname{Hom}(U,\ker a)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(M,j_*V')=\operatorname{Hom}_H(V,V')$, using [lem-per-trait-sheaf-gluing]. Both $i_*$ and $j^*$ are exact. Hence [lem-trf-bounded-below-derived-adjunction] identifies $Ri^!K$ with termwise $i^!J=\ker a$, its counit with the kernel inclusion, and the derived open unit with $g:J\to j_*j^*J$. These also compute the unbounded operations here: $J$ is K-injective by [lem-weil-pbc-bounded-below-injectives-kinjective], and right adjoints of exact functors preserve K-injectives by [lem-weil-pbc-right-adjoint-preserves-kinjective]. Thus $L=i_*i^!J$ and $E=j_*j^*J$ model the outer vertices of [lem-exc-closed-support-triangle], with the stated counit and unit. Step 8 proves $g$ surjective in every degree, so $0\to L\to J\xrightarrow{g}E\to0$ is exact. Exact $W$ sends it to Step 8's sequence.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text:
Here is the elementary kernel-to-cone computation, valid both for Step 9's sheaf sequence and its global-section sequence. For a degreewise epimorphism $g:J\to E$ with kernel $L$, put $H_g=\operatorname{Cone}(g)[-1]$, as in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Then
$$H_g^r=E^{r-1}\oplus J^r,\quad d(b,z)=(-db-gz,dz),\qquad \alpha:L\to H_g,\quad h\mapsto(0,h).$$
The quotient $H_g/\alpha(L)$ identifies termwise with $E^{r-1}\oplus E^r$, with differential $(b,c)\mapsto(-db-c,dc)$. The degree-minus-one map $(b,c)\mapsto(0,-b)$ contracts it: $dh+hd=\mathrm{id}$. Thus the quotient is acyclic. The long exact sequence of [lem-weil-pbc-complex-ses-homology-long-exact] gives $0\to H^r(L)\xrightarrow{H^r\alpha}H^r(H_g)\to0$ for every $r$, proving $\alpha$ a quasi-isomorphism. The explicit fibre triangle is the inverse rotation of the cone triangle in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]:
$$H_g\xrightarrow{p}J\xrightarrow{g}E\xrightarrow{i}H_g[1].$$
Transporting its first vertex by $\alpha$ defines the third map $E\to L[1]$ as $\alpha[1]^{-1}i$; it fixes the original inclusion $L\to J$ and quotient $g$. Every map just displayed is natural in maps of the short exact sequences.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text:
For Step 9 the cone-built triangle of Step 10 has exactly the counit and unit of [lem-exc-closed-support-triangle]. The third arrow of that specified triangle is unique. Indeed $j^*\dashv Rj_*$ identifies
$$\operatorname{Hom}(i_*Ri^!K[1],Rj_*j^*K)=\operatorname{Hom}(j^*i_*Ri^!K[1],j^*K)=0,$$
because [lem-exc-derived-open-closed-vanishing] applies to the disjoint immersions $i,j$ (and exact $i_*$ agrees with $Ri_*$). Clause (3) of [lem-weil-pbc-triangle-morphism-extension] therefore identifies that third arrow with $\alpha[1]^{-1}i$ from Step 10. Applying exact $W$ termwise carries $H_g^r=E^{r-1}\oplus J^r$ to $\operatorname{Cone}(Wg)[-1]^r$ with the identical differential; it sends $\alpha(h)=(0,h)$, $p$, and $i$ to those same three formulas for the global sequence. As $W$ preserves quasi-isomorphisms, it also sends $\alpha^{-1}$ to $(W\alpha)^{-1}$. Hence $W$ carries the actual third localization arrow to the cone-built third arrow of Step 8's global sequence, not merely its first two arrows. Step 8 identifies $W$ here with derived global sections.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text:
Let $B=\Gamma(\eta,J|_\eta)$, $g:W(J)\to B$ be restriction, and $e:B\to C(J)$ the augmentation of Step 5. Then $eg=r_J$. On shifted cones this gives
$$\phi:H_g\to H_{r_J},\qquad (b,w)\mapsto(e b,w).$$
It commutes with projections to $W(J)$ and with inclusions from $B$ and $C(J)$. It is a quasi-isomorphism: its two columns are $e$ and the identity of $W(J)$, so [lem-sc-integer-finite-column-total-comparison] applies; equivalently compare the long exact sequences of $0\to B[-1]\to H_g\to W(J)\to0$ and $0\to C(J)[-1]\to H_{r_J}\to W(J)\to0$ and use the five lemma. By Step 10, $\alpha:\Gamma_{\{s\}}(T,J)\to H_g$, $h\mapsto(0,h)$, is a quasi-isomorphism. Under Step 2's chain isomorphism $F(J)\to H_{r_J}$, the composite $\phi\alpha$ is exactly $h\mapsto(h,0,0)$. This proves that the augmentation prescribed in this item's statement is a quasi-isomorphism and gives the supported-vertex identification, without taking any normalization from the residue-model statement. The cone triangles from [def-weil-abstract-derived-category] commute on all arrows under $\phi$, including the last inclusion $i$, so Step 11 identifies them with global localization. The maps on the three vertices are the identity under the now specified identifications. Finally invert $K\to J$: $W,C$ are exact, and $F$ preserves quasi-isomorphisms by [lem-per-prime-power-trait-residue-model]. All augmentations and cone maps are natural; thus the statement holds naturally for every bounded below $K$.

source.place: Expose XVII, 1.2.1–1.2.2, printed pp. 259–260; chain-level expansion of Proposition 1.2.2.1

proof.text:
Finally use Step 2’s explicit chain isomorphism with the shifted cone of $r_K$ and the inverse rotation of its cone triangle in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], with rotation as in [def-weil-triangulated-category]. With the cone convention of [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], the fibre triangle is $F(K)\xrightarrow{q}W(K)\xrightarrow{r_K}C(K)\xrightarrow{-\iota[1]}F(K)[1]$. The last map in coordinates is
$$b(v,x)=(0,-v,x).$$
It is a chain map: $-D_F b(v,x)=(0,-dv,tv-dx)=bD_C(v,x)$. In particular a cocycle $(0,x)\in C(K)^{m+1}$ maps to $(0,0,x)\in F(K)^{m+2}$, so here $\epsilon_0=+1$. The cone comparison of Step 12 and localization identification of Step 11 identify this with the localization boundary, with identity on the three vertices. Changing the overall cone convention changes this formula by the single global sign coming from rotation; it introduces no dependence on $T$, $K$, $m$, or a generator. Every displayed map uses the augmentation ideal itself and no chosen generator. This proves (b), including its last cocycle formula.
